newsitem.title: CHINA: Weak imports help soaring China trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: Weak imports help soaring China trade surplus.

text.p: China's soaring trade surplus this year was based on weak demand that slowed imports coupled with policies to boost exports, but the imbalance was expected to narrow over the rest of the year, economists said on Friday.

"The credit squeeze has resulted in a delay in kicking off infrastructure projects, so demand for related goods has been reduced," Mao Yushi, a consultant at Unirule Institute of Economics, told Reuters.
China imposed a credit clampdown in 1993 to cool its overheating economy and only began a slight easing with two interest rate cuts last year.

The trade surplus for the first seven months widened to $20.53 billion compared with $1.965 billion in the year-ago period. Exports totalled $96.40 billion, up 26.1 percent year-on-year while imports rose only 1.9 percent to $75.86 billion.

The surplus in July alone was $2.76 billion, down from a surplus of $4.153 billion in June and $3.387 billion in May -- indicating that the huge gap between exports and imports may have begun to narrow.
"On the other hand, this (widened surplus) is a result of China's reform of its foreign trade system," Mao said.
China has in recent years implemented reforms allowing more enterprises to export their goods independent of state export firms and speeded up payment of export tax rebates, economists said.
Previously, only state-owned foreign trading houses were authorised to conduct exports.

Another factor boosting exports has been lacklustre domestic demand that has forced more enterprises to try to sell their goods abroad to ensure a profit, said an economist at the State Information Centre (SIC) under the State Planning Commission.
Imports were also limited by non-tariff barriers such as quotas on imports and the need to obtain licences for some goods, economists said.
However, the surplus was unlikely to widen much further in the second half of this year due in part to the strength of the domestic currency, the yuan.

The yuan has been appreciating steadily against the dollar in recent months, partly because of China's mounting foreign exchange reserves, which have risen by $21 billion from the start of 1997 to $126 billion at end-July.
"The surplus for the entire year should reach around $26 billion," said the SIC economist, who declined to be identified.
China's exports in the rest of the year would also be capped by competition from Southeast Asian nations, whose export ability has been boosted by the depreciation of their currencies, he said.

Exports by state-owned firms totalled $54.49 billion in January-July, up 25.7 percent year-on-year, while exports by foreign-funded businesses soared 24.9 percent to $39.23 billion, the customs figures showed.
Imports by state-owned firms were $32.83 billion, down 2.3 percent, while imports by foreign-funded companies rose 6.9 percent to $41.08 billion, the figures showed.
Exports of machinery and electronic products exceeded imports for the first time, rising 24.6 percent to $30.56 billion to account for 32 percent of total export volume.
